Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic errors in the model forecasts compared to true outcomes.

Looking at the examples, they all appear to be very similar - essentially the same data just shifted by one day. This suggests they're building up a dataset of forecast vs actual errors.

Let me analyze the patterns:

**Example 1 (2025-06-18):**
- History: prices around 70.41-75.94, generally trending up from earlier lows
- Sentiment: mix of positive (0.67, 1.00) and negative (-0.33, 0.00)
- Model forecasts: start at 74.60 on day 1, then 72.76, 73.21, 73.62, 74.01, 71.81, 71.31, 71.79, 69.99, 71.85, 73.58, 74.20, 74.35, 74.47, 74.06, 74.41, 75.23, 75.43, 75.36, 76.29, 75.82, 74.51, 73.31, 72.65, 71.24, 70.59, 71.01, 70.16, 68.21, 69.04

- True outcomes: 74.61, 72.74, 72.97, 73.27, 73.54, 71.15, 70.40, 70.96, 68.97, 70.58, 71.93, 72.06, 71.67, 71.20, 70.42, 70.39, 70.74, 70.55, 70.42, 71.51, 71.31, 70.55, 69.89, 69.83, 69.11, 69.36, 70.88, 71.34, 70.65, 73.08

Looking at the differences:


I notice the model's initial forecast is remarkably close to the first true outcome, with only a tiny 0.01 variance. However, as the timeline progresses, the predictions become increasingly inaccurate. The model struggles to accurately track price movements, particularly after the first few days when forecasts diverge significantly from actual prices.
